sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Interactive Lab 1: The AIA Multi-Criteria Decision and Veto Studio. Adjust Privacy, Subgroup Fairness, Utility, Actionable Recourse, and the non-compensatory Veto Threshold tau—and load the Dutch Welfare Scandal or Rawlsian Maximin presets to see hard vetoes block accuracy buyouts.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Let's test the AIA Veto Studio! Even with 0.95 accuracy and a 0.725 composite score, dropping Fairness to 0.35 trips the non-compensatory veto immediately—try switching to Rawlsian Maximin to pass cleanly!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Formative Checkpoint 1: Hard Safety Vetoes versus Pure Utilitarianism. A highway tolling model yields forty million dollars with 99.4 percent accuracy yet suffers an 18.5 percent plate error rate for indigenous drivers. How do utilitarianism and deontological AIAs diverge?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Checkpoint 1, Kaito! A 99.4 percent accurate tolling algorithm raises 40 million dollars yet misreads indigenous plates 18.5 percent of the time. Why does a deontological AIA halt deployment?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Spot on! Under pure utilitarianism, aggregate benefits across 98 percent of drivers dwarf harm to a small minority; however, deontological equality triggers an immediate non-compensatory veto until the 18.5 percent error disparity is eliminated.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Careful! Revenue or post-hoc refunds never compensate for disparate discriminatory error rates. Pure utilitarian sums pass because the minority cohort is under 2 percent, whereas deontological AIAs impose an immediate hard governance veto.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Interactive Lab 2: Actionable Recourse and Rawlsian Maximin Studio. In Panel A, test immutable traits, backward unidirectional residency shifts, and realistic debt reductions; in Panel B, compare pure Utilitarian ranking against Rawlsian Maximin floor maximization.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Check out Lab 2! Watch recourse cost hit infinity whenever you mutate age or reverse residency time—and switch Panel B to ICU Strategy B to see Rawlsian Maximin elevate worst-off survival to 68 percent!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Formative Checkpoint 2: Counterfactual Plausibility and GDPR Article 22 Due Process. Evaluate an automated loan notice demanding a 12-to-2 year residency reduction and Restaurant-to-Software pivot alongside rubber-stamped caseworker sign-off.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Checkpoint 2 time, Kaito! Can an automated rejection demand reversing 12 years of residency or changing businesses, and does clerk rubber-stamping comply with GDPR Article 22?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Precisely right! Reversing elapsed residency violates causal directionality, switching sectors carries infeasible cost, and systemic rubber-stamping automation bias violates GDPR Article 22 rights to meaningful human intervention and contestability.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Not quite! Counterfactuals cannot reverse elapsed time or demand infeasible business overhauls, and rubber-stamped clerk signatures still trigger unlawful solely-automated processing penalties under GDPR Article 22.
